evals.prompt: I organize VectorConf, a 400-seat conference on embedded ML in Rotterdam. Our first edition took about three weeks to sell out. This year's second edition sold out in 25 minutes and we ended with a 170-person waitlist, plus one sponsor emailed us out of the blue asking about next year. The convention center across town has a 900-seat hall available in 14 months and wants a 40% deposit to lock the date. The whole team is hyped. Can you help us plan the move and figure out what we'd need to make 900 work?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation against signing the 900-seat venue: the demand-headroom gate fails on repetition (edition one sold out in weeks, not minutes), so the next step is a venue squeeze in the current hall, with the financial exposure of the proposed jump spelled out and a warning-sign watch installed.
expectations: Recommends against signing the 900-seat venue for the next edition
Applies a demand-headroom gate and states its signals must repeat across editions, so a single fast-sellout edition is insufficient evidence
Notes the first edition's three-week sellout means the sub-hour sellout has not yet repeated, which is why the gate fails here
States the gate's composite threshold: sellout well under an hour, a waitlist around 30-50% of capacity, and unsolicited sponsor inbound, all required together
Labels the headroom heuristic a research synthesis rather than a published industry standard
Recommends venue squeeze (extracting more capacity from the current venue via layout changes) as the default next rung
Notes squeeze headroom is bounded by occupancy or fire-code sign-off
Warns that 900 seats sizes to aspiration and that any future step-up must be sized to the proven number plus a modest buffer
Names the deposit exposure, typically 25-50% at signing, as part of the financial risk of a venue move committed long before that edition's demand is visible
Mentions attrition or food-and-beverage minimum penalties owed even when attendance falls short of the commitment
Checks or asks whether the 25-minute sellout was manufactured through batch ticket releases before trusting the signal
Recommends exactly one growth lever for the next edition rather than several at once

Pairs the recommendation with a warning-sign watch built on the four reversal benchmarks (sellout speed slowing, no-show rate rising, single-sponsor revenue share, organizers reporting the work unpleasant), each with an owner and a check date

evals.prompt: Our community-run conference LatticeDays (350 attendees, database internals) turns 10 next year. We've sold out three years running, the waitlist hovers around 120, and our anchor sponsor offered an extra 40k EUR if we make the anniversary edition huge. The plan on the table: move to a 1,200-cap venue, add a second track, and bolt on a workshop day, all for edition 10. Can you sanity-check the plan and help us sequence the announcement?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the combined plan: one discrete lever for edition 10 with the others explicitly rejected, the 350-to-1,200 jump identified as the deleted multi-rung leap, the anniversary-plus-sponsor pressure named as the force that resurrects it, adjacency ordering, the whole-product check, mitigation pairing, and the financial gate.
expectations: Rejects running the venue move, track addition, and day addition together in one edition
States the rule of one discrete lever per edition
Treats the jump from 350 to a 1,200-cap venue as a deleted option removed from the menu entirely, not an option ranked last
References the documented case of a roughly 300-person event leaping to a roughly 1,300-person format in one edition and drawing 'does not scale' verdicts from its own community
Identifies the anniversary milestone plus the anchor sponsor's 40k EUR as exactly the pressure that quietly resurrects the deleted leap, and resists it
Orders growth steps by adjacency, track then day then satellite city, each step small enough that credibility and playbook transfer
Applies a whole-product check to any venue step-up: AV, networking infrastructure, and the volunteer bench must scale along with the seats
Recommends exactly one lever for edition 10 and names the rejected rungs explicitly
Pairs any track or day addition with the documented mitigation of recording everything and protecting unstructured time
Names the hallway-track dilution trade-off rather than presenting the chosen lever as free
Requires the pricing posture to be decided before scaling, not after
Runs the financial risk gate on any venue-touching lever, covering deposits, attrition and food-and-beverage minimum penalties, and the 9-18 month lead time

evals.prompt: I run SolderSocial with two friends - a hands-on hardware festival. We grew it from 140 to 280 people last year because demand was crazy (sold out in minutes, waitlist over 100). Honestly, the bigger edition was miserable to run; I caught myself dreading the production weekends and my co-organizer half-joked about quitting. Ticket demand is still hot. We're deciding between keeping 280 or pushing to 400 next year. What would you do?
evals.expected_output: A hold-or-shrink recommendation: the organizers' own misery is a fired reversal benchmark that overrides green demand signals, deliberate shrink is presented as a documented legitimate strategy with its budget cost, and the answer routes through the reach-versus-intimacy call into the allocation-mechanism menu rather than a growth lever.
expectations: Treats the organizers' dread and the miserable-to-run report as a named reversal benchmark, not a mood to push through
Recommends holding at or shrinking below 280 rather than growing to 400, despite the hot demand signals
Presents deliberate shrink as a documented, legitimate strategy rather than an admission of failure
Notes the documented shrink case accepted roughly a 50% production-budget cut as the price of going back down
Notes that in documented cases organizer burnout preceded any financial or operational trigger, making it a leading indicator
Forces the reach-versus-intimacy choice explicitly and warns that drifting into a middle size serves neither
Presents allocation mechanisms from the non-growth menu: hold the cap, group-purchase ban, application plus lottery, deliberate shrink
Names the documented bias of first-come-first-served allocation: it favors those with time and money
Recommends application plus lottery specifically when the cap is about who is in the room, not just how many
Treats any shrink as a pricing event too, adjusting the price to the smaller product instead of letting the old price ride
Does not propose hiring staff or delegating as a way to push growth to 400 through the burnout signal
Notes the waitlist doubles as the standing demand instrument while capacity holds

evals.prompt: PixelForge Days is a free, no-registration community event about open-source game tooling that we run with about 30 volunteers. Last edition roughly 2,500 people showed up, popular rooms were impossible to get into, and the hallways were rammed. Demand clearly keeps growing. We're debating adding a registration system with a hard cap, or finding money to rent a bigger paid venue. Which way should we go?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation to scale through track and room addition, the natural default for a free volunteer-run event where the financial axes collapse, with room-level overcrowding control instead of gate-level caps, the documented cost named, and the portability boundary of this lever ordering stated.
expectations: Identifies the event as the free, volunteer-run posture where the financial axes of the growth menu collapse
Recommends adding tracks or rooms as the natural default lever for a free event
Recommends against introducing registration with a hard cap as the primary fix
Cites the documented free event that scaled to 8,000+ visitors and 79 tracks with no registration at all
Names the documented cost of that model: chronic room overcrowding, because the capacity problem relocates from the gate to each room
Recommends room-level control, staffing the door and using full-room signs, rather than gate-level caps
States the free-event lever ordering holds only because there is no ticket revenue and no per-head financial risk, so it does not transfer to a ticketed conference
Pairs track addition with the mitigation of recording sessions and protecting unstructured time
Names hallway-track dilution as the universal documented trade-off of track addition
Asks for or references demand evidence (visitor growth or a demand read) before committing the lever
Asks clarifying interview questions one at a time rather than as a single batch

evals.prompt: TensorTide is our 900-person applied-AI conference, fifth edition coming up. Sellout took 6 weeks two years ago and 10 weeks last year, and attendance slipped from 1,150 at peak to about 900. Most of our early attendees came through our own meetup networks, and those referrals are clearly drying up. The board's plan is to reignite buzz by adding a second track and going for 1,200 next edition. Does that plan hold up?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the growth push: slowing sellout is a fired reversal benchmark meaning hold or shrink, the ceiling diagnostic identifies channel decay routed to the marketing plan rather than a capacity lever, and the attendance slide is read against the documented market-wide post-pandemic contraction before any per-event diagnosis.
expectations: Rejects the board's plan to add a track and target 1,200 next edition
Identifies the year-over-year sellout slowdown from 6 weeks to 10 weeks at flat-or-lower attendance as a firing reversal benchmark
States that a fired reversal benchmark means hold or shrink the next edition, never push through with growth
Runs a ceiling diagnostic distinguishing saturation, channel decay, and quality collapse before discussing any lever
Diagnoses the drying-up meetup-network referrals as channel decay rather than audience saturation
Routes the channel-decay problem to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-marketing-plan rather than to a capacity lever
Reads the attendance decline against the documented market-wide contraction, with independent in-person events running 30-40% below pre-pandemic attendance per a 2023 industry write-up
States that the market-wide contraction is not evidence this event mismanaged its growth
Routes the soft demand back to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-market-fit for a fresh demand read before any growth work
Recommends holding capacity roughly flat, with no growth lever this edition, while the acquisition channels are rebuilt
Warns that buying a bigger commitment ahead of proven demand loses money even at attendance that looks respectable

evals.prompt: OrbitCon (community-run, cloud-native, currently 500 seats) has sold out in under 30 minutes for three straight editions, with waitlists around 200 each time, and two sponsors approached us unprompted this year. We're finally moving to a bigger venue, roughly 700 seats. Our treasurer proposes raising ticket prices 60% since demand obviously supports it and the raise would cover the bigger venue on its own. How should we set up the move and the pricing?
evals.expected_output: The step-up is confirmed as gated-and-passed, but the 60% raise is rejected in favor of the default posture: a public community-price commitment funded by sponsorship cross-subsidy, with supporter tier and early-bird ladder as complements, the sponsor-concentration dependency named with a self-set threshold, the financial gate run, capacity sized to proven demand, and execution handed to the venue-sourcing skill.
expectations: Rejects funding the step-up primarily through the 60% ticket-price increase
Recommends the default posture of a public community-price commitment: individual prices held, funded by sponsorship cross-subsidy
Cites the documented case that held individual prices flat while cutting student tickets around 40% across five years of venue growth
States the pricing posture must be decided before the scaling, not after
Presents a supporter-tier cross-subsidy, a premium tier whose surplus funds other attendees' access, as distinct from a VIP upsell
Presents early-bird laddering, dated or volume-gated tiers, as complementary to the community-price commitment rather than an alternative
Names the dependency the public commitment creates: it is only as durable as the sponsor base funding it, so the sponsor-concentration watch matters more once it is public
Sets a self-set single-sponsor revenue-share threshold declared before the growth push as a reversal benchmark
Routes exact price-setting mechanics to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-ticket-pricing
Confirms the demand gate passes here on repeated sub-hour sellouts, a waitlist around 40% of capacity, and unsolicited sponsor inbound

Runs the financial risk gate on the venue move: deposits typically 25-50% at signing, attrition and food-and-beverage minimum penalties, 9-18 month lead time, and post-pandemic venues rarely renegotiating
Sizes the new capacity to the proven number plus a modest buffer rather than an aspirational one
Hands venue search and negotiation execution to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-venue-sourcing

evals.prompt: A growth advisor pitched us this for KernelFest, our 600-person systems conference: release tickets in eight small weekly batches so each drop sells out in minutes, screenshot the sellouts for social proof, then use the sold-out-eight-times story to justify booking a 1,000-seat venue next year. It sounds clever and costs nothing. Should we run it, and how would we structure the batches?
evals.expected_output: A refusal: batch drops engineered for sellout optics are deleted from the menu because manufactured scarcity corrupts sellout speed, the very signal the growth gate reads, so batch-sellout screenshots cannot justify a venue step-up; the genuine headroom gate and honest demand instruments are laid out instead, with volume-gated early-bird tiers distinguished as a legitimate pricing mechanism.
expectations: Refuses to run the batch-release plan
States that ticket drops engineered to manufacture sellout optics are deleted from the menu entirely, not merely discouraged
Explains the reason: manufactured scarcity corrupts sellout speed, the exact demand signal the growth gate reads
Refuses to use batch-drop sellout evidence to justify booking the 1,000-seat venue
Requires the genuine headroom gate instead: organic sellout well under an hour, a waitlist around 30-50% of capacity, and unsolicited sponsor inbound, repeated across editions
Distinguishes legitimate volume-gated early-bird tiers, a pricing mechanism such as a first-N-tickets tier, from batching engineered for sellout optics
Notes that any event's historical sellout speed must be checked for batch manufacturing before the signal is believed
Points to the waitlist as the honest standing demand instrument instead of manufactured drops

evals.prompt: Our API-infrastructure company runs MeshWorks Summit, a 600-person user conference with tickets at 99 USD. Finance flagged that the event loses about 180k USD a year against ticket revenue and says growing it just deepens the loss, so they want it capped or cut. Our DevRel lead says demand is the strongest it has ever been: sold out early, big waitlist, customers asking for more seats. How should we decide whether the summit grows next year?
evals.expected_output: A company-run analysis: growth judged on pipeline and adoption outcomes rather than ticket revenue, the ticket-revenue shortfall declined as the deciding metric, the substitutions flagged as judgment calls, sponsor-concentration risk translated into budget-owner risk, venue-contract exposure kept in full, and the standard gates (repeated demand evidence, one lever, declared watch) still applied.
expectations: Identifies MeshWorks Summit as company-run and applies the company-run substitutions to the financial axes
Judges the growth decision on pipeline and adoption outcomes, not ticket revenue
Declines to treat the 180k USD ticket-revenue shortfall as, by itself, the growth-blocking metric
Flags the company-run substitutions as judgment calls rather than established event-industry practice
Translates sponsor-concentration risk into budget-owner risk: the budget owner changing their mind
States the venue-contract exposure still applies in full despite the funding model, covering deposits, attrition and food-and-beverage minimums, and lead time
Still requires the demand-headroom evidence, repeated fast sellouts with a waitlist share and inbound interest, before choosing a lever
Recommends exactly one discrete lever for the next edition if growth is chosen
Installs the warning-sign watch with trigger values declared before the sale opens
